opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the Enlightenment humanists got something deeply right, but they were working with very primitive tools. Think about what they had: pamphlets, letters that took weeks to cross the ocean, coffee houses, a few printing presses. And with that, they built constitutional democracy, the scientific method, institutions for disagreeing productively without killing each other. That's incredible. That's one of the greatest achievements in human history, honestly.

But they also didn't know a lot of things we know now. They had a pretty naive model of human psychology: the rational agent who just needs to be shown the right argument. We now know a lot more about cognitive biases, about how groups actually form beliefs, about incentive design, game theory, mechanism design, how institutions decay, how information spreads through networks. We have a much richer science of coordination than Locke or Madison ever had access to. They were basically doing social engineering by intuition and by reading history. Brilliant intuition, but intuition.

And then on the technology side, we have communication at basically zero cost, instantly, globally. We can aggregate information in ways that would have seemed like magic. Prediction markets, forecasting, deliberation platforms, cryptographic tools for verification and trust. In principle, we have everything we'd need to build coordination mechanisms vastly better than a bunch of guys in wigs arguing in Philadelphia.

The problem, and this is the thing that keeps me up at night, is that we've mostly pointed this technology in the opposite direction. We've built the most powerful information machinery in history and optimized it for engagement, for outrage, for capturing attention. We've made coordination harder, not easier. So it's not that the potential isn't there. The potential is enormous. It's that we haven't done the work. We haven't had our version of the Enlightenment project of saying: okay, given what we now know, how do we deliberately design institutions that let millions or billions of people actually reason together and make good decisions?

And that matters enormously right now, because we're facing problems like AI that are fundamentally coordination problems. Nobody individually wants to build something that kills everybody, but the race dynamics push everyone forward anyway. That's a coordination failure. And our current institutions are clearly not up to it. So I'm not saying we can do better than the Enlightenment because we're smarter than them. We're not. I'm saying we have better tools and more knowledge, and frankly we don't really have a choice. We have to do better, because the stakes are higher than they've ever been.

r003.rationale: It says Enlightenment thinkers relied on intuition and had a limited model of psychology, but does not argue that they used moral prescriptions to compensate for limited understanding of cooperation.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that the Enlightenment humanists were working with an incredibly impoverished picture of what humans actually are. And I don't say that as an insult, they did astonishingly well with what they had. But think about it: they didn't have game theory, they didn't have evolutionary biology, they didn't have cognitive science, they had basically no understanding of how brains work, how incentives shape institutions, how coordination problems actually fail. They were running on introspection and a handful of historical case studies. And yet they bootstrapped things like the scientific method, constitutional government, the idea that disagreement can be resolved by argument rather than by violence. That's a miracle, honestly.

But a lot of what they built was built on folk psychology. Locke and Rousseau and Kant were essentially guessing about human nature, and some of those guesses were wrong. The assumption that people are basically rational agents who will converge on truth if you just give them free speech and a printing press, that's a lovely idea, and it's partly true, but we now know a lot about why it fails. We know about motivated reasoning, we know about tribal signalling, we know about how information cascades work, we know about Goodhart's law and how any metric you optimize for gets gamed. We have actual mathematical models of when cooperation is stable and when it collapses, Ostrom's work on commons, mechanism design, all of this.

So the way I'd frame it is: the Enlightenment gave us a prototype, a sort of version one of large-scale voluntary cooperation among strangers. And it's been degrading, in my view, partly because the environment changed faster than the institutions did. The printing press was one thing. Twitter is a completely different thing. The institutions weren't designed for an adversarial information environment where attention is the scarce resource and you have optimization processes, both human and increasingly algorithmic, actively searching for exploits in human cognition.

And that's where the "improve on" part comes in. We're not smarter than Hume, individually. But we have tools he didn't have. We can run experiments on institutional design. We can actually model the dynamics. We can build cryptographic systems that let people verify things without trusting a central authority. We can, in principle, build AI systems that help people reason better rather than worse, although right now the default trajectory is very much the opposite, which is sort of my whole thing.

The thing I'd really emphasize, though, is that this is a choice. None of this happens automatically. Technology doesn't make us more cooperative by default; if anything the default is that it gets used to extract and manipulate, because that's where the money is. So improving on the Enlightenment isn't something that's going to happen to us. It's an engineering project, and it's a civilizational engineering project, and we've barely started taking it seriously. We treat our institutions like weather instead of like things we built and can rebuild. The humanists at least understood that part. They knew they were designing something. We've kind of forgotten that.

astra-6.text:
I think the Enlightenment humanists had a very important insight, which is that people with different beliefs can still find ways to live together and cooperate. You don’t have to agree about everything to benefit from having some shared rules. But they were working with a much more limited understanding of how people think, how institutions work, and how information spreads.

We now have tools like game theory and a much better understanding of coordination problems. You can have a situation where everyone individually behaves reasonably, and the outcome is terrible for everyone. Understanding that lets you ask a more useful question than “How do we make everybody a better person?” You can ask, “How do we change the incentives so that cooperation actually makes sense?”

And technology gives us more ways to implement those ideas—to communicate, to check claims, to make commitments that other people can verify. That doesn’t mean technology automatically produces cooperation. It can make manipulation and conflict easier too. But we have more knowledge and more tools available. The opportunity is to use those deliberately to build institutions where people can cooperate even when they disagree, even when they don’t particularly trust each other.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the Enlightenment humanists had a really important insight: people who disagree profoundly can still build institutions that let them cooperate. You don’t have to settle every religious or philosophical question before you can make life better together.

But they were working with a pretty limited understanding of how humans actually think. We now have psychology, game theory, computer science—tools for understanding incentives, coordination failures, and the ways our own reasoning goes wrong. And we have communication technology that lets people find one another and collaborate at a scale they couldn’t have imagined.

That doesn’t automatically make us wiser. The same technology can amplify conflict and manipulation. But it gives us the possibility of deliberately designing better systems for cooperation. We can ask: where does this institution fail? What incentives does it create? How could we make it easier for people to tell the truth, trust one another, and correct mistakes? We don’t have to assume the Enlightenment was the final word. We can take that project seriously enough to improve it.
